abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO® brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright.

sections.body: The paper argues that coding agents need tools for assembling builds and checking physical feasibility. Multi-part assemblies must use preset parts, avoid collisions and floating parts, and usually form one connected component. The proposed toolkit has two parts: an assembly API and a validator that gives feedback on physical validity. The authors focus on LEGO brick builds. They report that GPT-6 Astra with Codex writes scripts to generate and validate its output more than 80% of the time (Appendix D), yet its builds still contain colliding, floating, or disconnected parts (Fig. 2). Existing 3D toolkits target digital assets and do not consider physical constraints. The paper introduces BrickLayer and BrickWright to address this gap.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Coding agents often produce invalid brick assemblies, so this paper proposes a toolkit with an assembly API and a validator.

sections.body: Earlier optimization and retrieval methods are limited by small brick vocabularies, explicit geometric guidance, or fixed templates. Learning-based methods such as BrickGPT and LEGO-Maker are restricted to specific brick types, orientations, or categories. LegoACE can produce disconnected components, and BrickNet accumulates collisions over longer build sequences. Physics-aware methods use force-based stability analysis or physics simulation, or refine outputs after generation. The paper states that BrickWright uses pre-trained models without task-specific training and checks collisions and connectivity in a feedback loop. Agentic 3D work such as Articraft targets digital assets, while BrickWright assembles fixed parts whose connectors determine how they attach.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior brick generation relies on small vocabularies or fixed templates, while agentic 3D tools do not consider physical constraints.

sections.body: A build is an ordered sequence of placements of catalog elements or nested builds, each with a rigid transform. It is valid if it uses only catalog parts and has no colliding or floating parts. A physically feasible build is valid and has as few connected components as possible. BrickLayer provides part search, typed connectors, mating, and validation. BrickWright gives a single agent a lightweight harness in which it writes build.py with `create_build()` and `run_tests()`, then iterates with validate, render, and finalize. The system prompt contains only the BrickLayer documentation and the loop, with no planning advice or example builds. Stability and executable assembly sequences are left to future work.
sections.heading: BrickWright
sections.headline: BrickWright has an agent write Python build code with BrickLayer, validating collisions, floaters, and connectivity in a plan-execute-validate loop.

sections.body: Baselines include the specialized models BrickGPT and BrickNet and the agentic methods Articraft, Codex, and Claude Code. Evaluation uses BrickNet-512, which has 512 text prompts. Lightweight agents are Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna; GPT-6.1 Sol is balanced and GPT-6 Astra is frontier. Table 1 shows full BrickWright reaching 1.000 valid builds for every agent. Lightweight Haiku and Luna gain prompt adherence, and stronger agents maintain it. Ablations show the validator is necessary: without it, all agents score below 79% validity. Agentic methods have a budget of USD 5 per sample, and the latest completed build is used when the budget is reached.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: BrickWright raises validity to 100% on 512 prompts, with Luna rising from 9% to 100% and prompt adherence held or improved.

sections.body: The discussion states that even the most capable agents fail to produce physically feasible builds much of the time. BrickWright is presented as a toolkit for brick build creation and validation. Lightweight agents reach 100% validity on 512 samples while improving prompt adherence at a similar cost to agents without BrickWright. The stated limitations are that the feasibility definition excludes valid assembly sequences and stability analysis, and that agentic methods are generally slower and more costly than specially trained models. Distilling agent capabilities into smaller, faster models is named as a future direction. The authors hope the work highlights well-written construction APIs and physical validation.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Lightweight agents reach 100% validity, but feasibility excludes stability and assembly sequences, and agents run slower and costlier.

sections.body: Appendix A reports `valid@k`, the fraction of builds whose first k validate calls include a passing call, along with token use. For example, 81% of GPT-6.1 Sol builds pass within two calls, compared with 37% without the assembly API. Table 2 breaks down validation failures: physical checks account for 63–85% of failures, mostly collisions for GPT agents and connectivity for Haiku. Appendix B gives the system prompt and BrickLayer reference. Appendix C lists example prompts for the figures. Appendix D reports that 471 of 512 Codex builds use a generator and 424 use a validator.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists valid@k results, validation failure breakdowns, prompts, the system prompt and API reference, and vanilla agent analysis.
